PLASTIBLENDS INDIA Q2 : REVENUE GROWTH DESPITE HIGH RAW MATERIAL & ENERGY COSTS

• Company reported revenue growth despite challenging market conditions, supported by improved price realisations.

• Raw Material & Operating Costs: Elevated raw material prices, power and freight expenses continued to pressure profitability.

• Gujarat Power Costs: Fuel surcharge increased significantly during Q2, further raising manufacturing costs.

• Margin Outlook: Company absorbed part of the higher costs to protect customers and market share. Management plans to pass these costs on in subsequent quarters.

• Exports: Export business performed well, supported by entry into new markets and an improved product mix.

• Rupee Depreciation: INR weakened to approximately ₹96/USD from ₹88/USD a year ago, improving export competitiveness but increasing import costs.

• Engineering Plastics: Division continues to grow, with management expecting strong momentum ahead.

• Solar Expansion: Commissioned a 5.2 MW solar open-access power project in Gujarat in September 2026 to help offset higher energy costs.

• Management Outlook: Focus remains on cost optimisation, operational efficiency, export growth and sustainable expansion.

ZYDUSLIFE : PRESENTS NEW POST HOC EPICS-III DATA FOR SAROGLITAZAR IN PBC

• Post hoc analysis of the Phase 3 EPICS-III trial presented at ACG 2026 by Zydus Therapeutics, a wholly owned subsidiary of Zydus Lifesciences
• Composite biochemical response rates greater with saroglitazar than placebo in both U.S. (60.7% vs 0%) and non-U.S. subgroups (55.1% vs 13.5%)
• Larger treatment difference in the U.S. subgroup (delta 60.7%) versus non-U.S. (delta 41.6%)
• ALP normalization treatment difference at Week 52 similar between U.S. and non-U.S. subgroups (7.7% vs 9.6%)
• Saroglitazar generally well tolerated; most common adverse reactions were pruritus, headache and urinary tract infection
• Saroglitazar is under FDA review; if approved, Zydus Therapeutics plans to launch it in the United States by March 2027
Impact: Positive (Strengthens the clinical profile of saroglitazar in PBC ahead of a possible U.S. launch, though the product remains investigational and the analysis is exploratory)

Business Overview

Proposed Demerger & Restructuring
- February 2026 board-approved scheme proposes business transfers to Religare Finvest.

- Religare Enterprises would become a pure-play health insurance holding company.
- Completion target: 15–18 months from February 2026.

- Operating scale is expected to support underwriting improvement.
- Medical inflation and competitive group pricing remain challenges.

Religare Housing Finance

- FY26 loss stood at ₹18.6 Cr on ₹30 Cr income.
- Current monthly disbursements remain below ₹10 Cr.
- Profitability depends on scaling secured lending disbursements.

- Margin funding and third-party distribution are key growth initiatives.

- Lending recovery remains at an early stage.

Tarapur Manufacturing Expansion
- INDIFLIN technical manufacturing line targeted for completion by March 2027.

Specialty Product Growth
- Excalia Max and Lentigo exceeded FY26 internal targets.

- These products could support specialty revenue growth in FY27.
- Performance remains sensitive to weather conditions.

Profitability & Margins

- Excalia Max and Lentigo growth could face weather disruptions.

THE NEW INDIA ASSURANCE COMPANY LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW

Business Overview

- Offers health, fire, motor, marine, liability, aviation and crop insurance.
- Health and personal accident contribute 48.16% of premiums.
- Fire contributes 15.52% of premiums.
- Motor third-party contributes 13.04% of premiums.
- Government-owned insurer with operations across India and 24 countries.
- Designated a Domestic Systemically Important Insurer (D-SII).

Combined Ratio Improvement
- FY26 internal target: Around 113% combined ratio.
- Q1 FY26 combined ratio stood at 116.16%.
- Management targets approximately 3% improvement during FY26.
- Lower combined ratios could reduce underwriting losses.
- Better underwriting performance could improve return on equity.

Health Insurance Profitability
- Overall health loss ratio target: 98–100%.
- Q3 FY26 health ICR improved from 103% to 91%.
- Health represents 48.16% of total premiums.
- Sustained improvement could materially support combined ratio reduction.
- Retail health pricing remains constrained by IRDAI regulations.

ROE & New Opportunities
- Nine-month FY26 ROE stood at 4.95%.
- Management targets double-digit ROE.
- Lower incurred claim ratios are the primary improvement lever.
- Parametric insurance is gaining traction.
- Around 10–12 parametric insurance contracts have been completed.

Key Risks
- Motor TP premiums have not been revised since 2022.
- Motor TP ICR stood at 108.2% in FY25.
- Retail health premium increases are capped at 10% annually.
- Medical inflation remains elevated at 14–15%.
- Air India aviation claim pushed aviation ICR to 323% for 9M FY26.
- Marine ship-sinking claims raised marine ICR to 119% in Q3 FY26.
- Wage revision arrears of approximately ₹2,500 Cr affected FY26.
- Additional family pension costs of ₹700–800 Cr were expected in Q4 FY26.
- These costs could increase the expense ratio.

Key Takeaway
- Health claims improvement is central to profitability recovery.
- Combined ratio reduction is critical for achieving double-digit ROE.
- Motor TP pricing and medical inflation remain structural challenges.
- Large claims and employee-related costs could create earnings volatility.

Business Overview

Growth Targets & Expansion
- FY28 related-party sales target: ₹13,500 million.
- Bharat Forge supply target: ₹6,500 million in FY28.
- Kalyani Technoforge supply target: ₹7,000 million in FY28.
- Combined target equals approximately 73% of FY26 revenue from operations.
- Approved single-source supplier status supports OEM-linked demand.
- KTFL target rises from ₹4,058.83 million in FY26.
- Merger of Kalyani Transmission Technologies into KTFL consolidated demand from April 1, 2024.

Capacity & Operational Considerations
- The 250,000 MT plant is operating near full capacity.

- Near-full capacity limits the ability to absorb incremental volumes.
- Customer concentration, raw material costs and governance require close monitoring.

- Merger aims to consolidate cable capacity and broaden product offerings.

- Birla Cable merger delays could disrupt consolidation plans.

- AI data centre demand is shifting capacity toward G657 A2 fibre.

- JJM funding recovery could revive the EPC business.
- Birla Cable merger could strengthen cable manufacturing capabilities.
- E-Beam expansion supports higher-value specialty cable opportunities.
- Government execution, merger approvals and input costs remain critical variables.

DCB BANK LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Private sector bank focused on secured, small-ticket lending.
- Core customers include small businesses, traders and farmers.
- Focus markets span Tier 2 to Tier 6 India.
- Key segments include mortgages, gold loans and agri lending.
- Mid-SME lending is being rebuilt.
- Corporate and construction finance exposure remains deliberately limited.
- Other income includes insurance, mutual fund distribution and trade finance.

Profitability Targets
- FY27 ROE target: 13.5%.
- FY28 ROE target: 14.5%.
- Q1 FY27 ROE already stood at 13.61%.
- Deposit repricing benefits support profitability.
- Mortgage disbursement momentum remains another key driver.

Loan Growth & Mortgage Business
- Management targets balance-sheet growth above 20–23% if momentum sustains.
- Q1 FY27 mortgage disbursements rose 35% YoY.
- Disbursements reached ₹1,500 Cr versus ₹1,100 Cr previously.
- Fresh mortgage sourcing is shifting towards higher-yield business loans.
- Sustained loan growth depends on funding availability and credit quality.

Capital Raise
- Proposed primary capital raise: ₹1,100–1,200 Cr.
- Expected timing: Late Q2 or early Q3 FY27.
- Enabling shareholder resolution permits fundraising up to ₹2,000 Cr.
- The resolution includes ₹1,500 Cr of Tier 1 capital.
- Capital aims to support growth while maintaining ROE targets.

Mid-SME Expansion
- Target loan sizes: ₹3–15 Cr.
- Presence is expanding from 4 to 10 locations.
- Meaningful loan-book contribution targeted within 3–4 quarters.
- Current-account acquisition and trade finance are also being rebuilt.
- Successful execution could improve fee income and funding diversification.

Financial Estimates
| Metric | FY27E | FY28E | FY29E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue (₹ Cr) | 3,910 | 4,731 | 5,725 |
| Revenue Growth | 18.1% | 21.0% | 21.0% |
| PAT (₹ Cr) | 944 | 1,158 | 1,490 |
| PAT Growth | 29.0% | 22.6% | 28.7% |
| Forward P/E | 7.8x | 6.4x | 5.0x |

Key Risks
- NIM expansion depends on deposit costs declining through Q2–Q3 FY27.
- Current-account growth was only 5% YoY in Q1 FY27.
- Gold loans represent approximately 20–22% of the loan book.
- Over 90% of co-lending is also gold-heavy.
- Co-lending partners source at 85% LTV versus 75% for organic lending.
- Sharp gold-price movements could increase collateral risk.
- Mid-SME expansion is being rebuilt from a small base.
- Execution delays could slow loan growth and fee-income recovery.

Key Takeaway
- Mortgage growth and deposit repricing support near-term profitability.
- Mid-SME expansion offers additional lending and fee-income opportunities.
- Capital raising could strengthen capacity for future growth.
- Deposit costs, gold collateral and execution remain key monitorables.

SUZLON ENERGY LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- India's largest wind energy solutions provider.
- Operates 14 domestic manufacturing facilities.
- Annual manufacturing capacity: 4.5 GW.
- Global installed base exceeds 21 GW.
- WTG segment supplies turbines and wind farm EPC services.
- RE AMS manages 16.1 GW of Indian wind assets.

- DevCo contributed 60% of order inflows during this period.

- Advanced development pipeline: 8–10 GW.
- DevCo packages developed sites with EPC contracts.

Long-Term Renewable Energy Targets
- Targeting 10 GW renewable energy sales by FY31.
- Planned energy mix: 75% wind and 25% non-wind.
- Target implies 7,500 MW annual wind deliveries.
- Current quarterly delivery rate: 506 MW.
- Existing 4.5 GW capacity could support 7.5 GW output.
- Transition to 5 MW turbines improves effective manufacturing output.

New Turbine Platforms
- S175 5 MW turbine secured its first Indian customer order.
- Deliveries are expected to begin by FY27-end.
- S163 6.3 MW turbine supports export market re-entry.
- Blue Sky platform targets international opportunities.
- Export revenue is expected from FY28.

Battery Storage Opportunity
- BESS target: 3.1 GW by FY31.
- Technology partnerships expected to close within months.
- Storage could complement wind and FDRE project packages.
- This creates an additional non-wind revenue opportunity.

| Metric | FY27E | FY28E | FY29E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

| PAT Growth | 26.2% | 37.0% | 32.5% |
| Forward P/E | 28.0x | 20.4x | 15.4x |

- Around 350 MW was grid-ready but faced evacuation constraints.
- DevCo revolving capital deployment is capped at ₹500 Cr.

- Slower EPC conversion could pressure working capital.
- Export orders remain unproven, with revenue expected from FY28.
- Firm orders for Europe, Australia and Latin America remain unannounced.
- PSU customers have longer payment cycles than private customers.
- Receivables stood at ₹5,700 Cr in Q3 FY26.
- ₹2,100 Cr was linked to incomplete milestones.

Key Takeaway
- EPC, DevCo and larger turbines support ambitious growth targets.
- BESS could diversify revenue beyond wind energy.
- Manufacturing capacity offers potential operating leverage.
- Commissioning delays and grid evacuation remain execution risks.
- Receivables, export traction and DevCo capital efficiency need monitoring.

MODISON LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Manufactures silver, copper and copper-tungsten electrical contacts.
- Products serve low, medium and high-voltage switchgear applications.
- India's only company covering the complete LV-to-HV range.
- Operates an in-house silver refinery, tool room and R&D centre.
- Supplies global OEMs including GE, Siemens, Hitachi, ABB and Schneider.
- Government customers include ISRO, BEL and BHEL.
- Also operates bullion and silver-compounds businesses.

Revenue Growth Targets
- FY28 revenue target: ₹1,000 Cr, advanced from the original 2030 plan.
- FY30 revenue target revised to ₹1,365 Cr.
- Growth drivers include LV and HV product expansion.
- 260 products were developed during FY26.
- New domestic customers and the ISRO alloy channel support expansion.

Export Growth
- FY27 export revenue target: ₹100 Cr.
- This would mark the first time exports cross ₹100 Cr.
- Growth targets 20–25 identified global customers.
- Existing channels through GE, Siemens and ABB support export opportunities.

ISRO Alloy Opportunity
- Developed a specialised brazing alloy previously sourced only from Russia.
- ISRO had faced unsuccessful attempts with 5–6 suppliers over 5–6 years.
- Modison has completed technology and material transfer documentation.
- This creates potential recurring supplies to India's space and defence ecosystem.

Key Risks
- Revenue depends heavily on a handful of global OEM groups.
- Sourcing-panel decisions can materially change order volumes.
- Silver represents 80–90% of LV material costs.
- Process metal inventory runs at 2–3x shipped volume.
- Silver-price volatility can increase working-capital and margin pressure.
- Silver fell from ₹70,000/kg to ₹54,000–55,000/kg in FY22.
- EBITDA margin declined to 6.95% in FY23.
- Tungsten supply constraints affected HV contacts during FY26.
- Tungsten cannot be hedged like silver.
- FY26 refinery fire caused ₹1,021.04 lakh costs over a 7–8-day shutdown.
- KEMA and CESI approvals must remain current as product designs evolve.

Key Takeaway
- LV/HV expansion and exports support ambitious revenue targets.
- The ISRO alloy offers a differentiated government-customer opportunity.
- Global OEM relationships provide access to international markets.
- Silver volatility, tungsten availability and customer concentration remain key risks.
- Product certifications and operational resilience are critical to execution.

GANESHA ECOSPHERE LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- India's largest PET recycler.
- Converts post-consumer PET waste into recycled polyester products.
- Recycled fibre and spun yarn contribute approximately 65% of revenue.
- Food-grade rPET granules contribute approximately 35% of revenue.
- rPET serves beverage and FMCG brands under EPR mandates.
- Operates six Indian facilities and one Nepal facility.
- Combined installed capacity: Approximately 2.18 lakh tonnes annually.
- Collection network exceeds 300 suppliers.
- Daily PET waste procurement: Approximately 450 tonnes.

FY27 Volume & EBITDA Targets
- Consolidated EBITDA target: ₹225–250 Cr.
- FY27 volume guidance: 1.8–2.0 lakh tonnes.
- Warangal rPET utilisation target: 85–90%.
- Final MoEF notification dated 31 March 2026 reinstated FY27's 40% recycled-content mandate.
- Higher utilisation depends on policy-led demand and regulatory approvals.

Warangal Capacity Expansion
- Target capacity: Approximately 97,000–98,000 tonnes by Q4 FY27.
- Commissioned brownfield line adds 22,500 tonnes.
- FSSAI approval was awaited by end-June 2026.
- Another 22,500-tonne line targets operation by Q4 FY27.
- Debottlenecking could add approximately 10,000 tonnes.
- Planned capex: Around ₹150 Cr.
- Expansion is expected to be internally funded.

Revenue Mix Transformation
- rPET revenue share target: 65% by FY28.
- rPET contributed approximately 35% as of Q2 FY26.
- Warangal filament yarn capacity is ramping up.
- A leading global textile brand is the key customer.
- Full utilisation was expected within 3–6 months from Q4 FY26.
- Filament yarn realisation: ₹150–160/kg.

Financial Estimates
| Metric | FY27E | FY28E | FY29E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue (₹ Cr) | 1,779 | 2,322 | 2,618 |
| Revenue Growth | 20.0% | 30.6% | 12.7% |
| PAT (₹ Cr) | 102 | 145 | 171 |
| PAT Growth | 167.6% | 42.1% | 17.7% |

Key Risks
- EPR demand remains dependent on regulatory policy.
- June 2025 draft rules previously froze brand offtake.
- Warangal utilisation fell to 50% in Q3 FY26.
- PET scrap prices reached ₹55–56/kg.
- Legacy fibre margins face imperfect cost pass-through.
- rPET EBITDA stood at ₹19.80/kg.
- This is below FY25 levels of ₹25–28/kg.
- Industry FSSAI-approved capacity could reach 7–7.5 lakh tonnes within two years.
- Rising industry capacity could intensify competition.

Key Takeaway
- Policy support and Warangal expansion could drive strong growth.
- rPET's rising revenue share could transform the business mix.
- Filament yarn adds higher-value product opportunities.

Premium Fans & BLDC Growth

Business Overview
- Manufactures exhaust and emission control systems.

Lightweighting Business
- FY26 control arms and links market share: Approximately 14%.
- Management targets further market-share gains during FY27.
- Existing orders carry combined annual value of approximately US$22 million.
- US$3 million annual order targets SOP in Q3 FY27.
- This order carries US$15 million lifetime value.
- Two additional orders carry US$14 million annual value.
- Their combined lifetime value is US$70 million.
- These orders target SOP in Q1 FY28.

Export Order Pipeline
- North American engine and genset orders total US$10.7 million annually.
- Lifetime value of these orders: US$58.5 million.
- Revenue conversion is expected from Q3 FY27.
- SOP slipped from Q2 FY27 due to customer inventory build-up.
- First European agricultural equipment OEM order secured.
- European order value: US$2 million annually and US$10 million lifetime.
- European order SOP is targeted for Q1 FY28.

Emission Regulations & Replacement Demand
- BS6.3 and WLTP apply from 1 April 2027.
- Regulations cover vehicles below 3.5 tonnes GVW.
- Multiple WLTP replacement orders secured in Q1 FY27.
- CAFE III requirements begin from April 2027.
- Demand opportunities span hybrids, CNG, ethanol and flex-fuel vehicles.
- Emission-system upgrades could support future replacement orders.

New Lightweighting Products
- Donghee technology licence signed in October 2025.
- Subframes and torsion beams planned from FY28.
- Incremental content opportunity: ₹4,000–10,000 per vehicle.
- Customer platform finalisation will determine commercial ramp-up.

- North American export orders have faced a two-quarter delay.
- Customer inventory and OEM schedules affect revenue conversion.
- US tariff policy remains uncertain.

- Current rules favour mufflers over full after-treatment systems.
- Lack of supply to India's largest PV OEM limits market-share gains.
- Catalyst price pass-through can distort reported revenue and margins.

Key Takeaway
- Lightweighting orders provide visibility for FY27–FY28 growth.
- Export orders offer diversification beyond domestic OEMs.
- WLTP and CAFE III could support emission-system demand.
- Subframes and torsion beams add future content-per-vehicle opportunities.
- Export delays, regulation changes and customer concentration remain key risks.

PETRONET LNG – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Operates India's largest LNG import and regasification business
- Dahej terminal capacity: 22.5 MMTPA
- Kochi terminal capacity: 5 MMTPA
- Handles roughly two-thirds of India's LNG imports
- Long-term LNG suppliers include QatarEnergy and ExxonMobil
- Promoter offtakers include GAIL, IOCL, BPCL and ONGC
- Revenue primarily comes from contracted regasification fees
- Expanding into petrochemicals and East Coast LNG infrastructure

Dahej Petrochemical Project
- Project includes 750 KTA propane dehydrogenation capacity
- Polypropylene capacity: 500 KTA
- Approved project capex: ₹20,685 Cr
- Commissioning targeted by 2028
- FY27 capex planned: ₹7,500 Cr
- Physical progress reported at 40%
- Deepak Phenolics offtake: 250 KTA propylene and 11 KTA hydrogen
- ONGC contract covers 600 KTPA

Gopalpur LNG Terminal
- Planned East Coast terminal capacity: 5 MMTPA
- Construction expected to begin in FY27
- Project remains subject to environmental clearance
- Construction timeline: Approximately three years
- Target utilisation: 80–90%

Kochi Terminal – Utilisation
- Current terminal capacity: 5 MMTPA
- Utilisation depends on pipeline connectivity
- GAIL pipeline completion expected in H1 FY27
- Pipeline connects Kochi with Bangalore and Mangalore
- ExxonMobil supply contract covers 1.2 MMTPA from FY27
- Better connectivity could improve terminal utilisation

Dahej Expansion & LNG Contracts
- Capacity expanded from 17.5 to 22.5 MMTPA
- Expansion mechanically completed around March 2026
- Capitalisation occurred in Q1 FY27
- New contracts being negotiated for incremental capacity
- Counterparties include GAIL, IOCL, BPCL, ONGC and Performance Chemieserve
- Performance Chemieserve contract: 0.5 MMTPA
- QatarEnergy's renewed 7.5 MMTPA contract starts in 2028
- Contract runs until 2048 on delivered terms
- Back-to-back offtake renewals targeted within 2–3 quarters

Financial Estimates

| Metric | FY27E | FY28E | FY29E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | ₹29,700 Cr | ₹38,190 Cr | ₹43,800 Cr |
| Revenue Growth | -31.7% | 28.6% | 14.7% |
| PAT | ₹3,976 Cr | ₹4,053 Cr | ₹4,409 Cr |
| PAT Growth | 1.6% | 1.9% | 8.8% |
| Forward P/E | 10.8x | 10.6x | 9.7x |

Key Risks
- Petrochemical project requires substantial execution and capex
- Expected project returns have not been specified
- Incremental Dahej capacity needs new cargoes and offtake contracts
- Kochi utilisation depends on timely pipeline completion
- Gopalpur terminal adds significant investment requirements
- Third jetty capex: ₹2,013 Cr
- Gopalpur terminal capex: ₹6,355 Cr
- QatarEnergy supply disruption could affect throughput
- Sustained LNG spot prices above $15–17/MMBtu could hurt demand

Key Takeaway
- Dahej expansion and new contracts support growth potential
- Petrochemicals offer diversification beyond regasification
- Kochi and Gopalpur provide additional utilisation opportunities
- FY27–FY29 estimates indicate modest PAT growth
- High capex and project execution remain key monitorables
- Contract renewals and LNG availability are critical

PETRONET LNG – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Operates India's largest LNG import and regasification business
- Dahej terminal capacity: 22.5 MMTPA
- Kochi terminal capacity: 5 MMTPA
- Handles roughly two-thirds of India's LNG imports
- Long-term LNG suppliers include QatarEnergy and ExxonMobil
- Promoter offtakers include GAIL, IOCL, BPCL and ONGC
- Revenue primarily comes from contracted regasification fees
- Expanding into petrochemicals and East Coast LNG infrastructure

Dahej Petrochemical Project
- Project includes 750 KTA propane dehydrogenation capacity
- Polypropylene capacity: 500 KTA
- Approved project capex: ₹20,685 Cr
- Commissioning targeted by 2028
- FY27 capex planned: ₹7,500 Cr
- Physical progress reported at 40%
- Deepak Phenolics offtake: 250 KTA propylene and 11 KTA hydrogen
- ONGC contract covers 600 KTPA

Gopalpur LNG Terminal
- Planned East Coast terminal capacity: 5 MMTPA
- Construction expected to begin in FY27
- Project remains subject to environmental clearance
- Construction timeline: Approximately three years
- Target utilisation: 80–90%

Kochi Terminal – Utilisation
- Current terminal capacity: 5 MMTPA
- Utilisation depends on pipeline connectivity
- GAIL pipeline completion expected in H1 FY27
- Pipeline connects Kochi with Bangalore and Mangalore
- ExxonMobil supply contract covers 1.2 MMTPA from FY27
- Better connectivity could improve terminal utilisation

Dahej Expansion & LNG Contracts
- Capacity expanded from 17.5 to 22.5 MMTPA
- Expansion mechanically completed around March 2026
- Capitalisation occurred in Q1 FY27
- New contracts being negotiated for incremental capacity
- Counterparties include GAIL, IOCL, BPCL, ONGC and Performance Chemieserve
- Performance Chemieserve contract: 0.5 MMTPA
- QatarEnergy's renewed 7.5 MMTPA contract starts in 2028
- Contract runs until 2048 on delivered terms
- Back-to-back offtake renewals targeted within 2–3 quarters

| Metric | FY27E | FY28E | FY29E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | ₹29,700 Cr | ₹38,190 Cr | ₹43,800 Cr |
| Revenue Growth | -31.7% | 28.6% | 14.7% |

| PAT Growth | 1.6% | 1.9% | 8.8% |
| Forward P/E | 10.8x | 10.6x | 9.7x |

- Petrochemical project requires substantial execution and capex
- Expected project returns have not been specified

- Kochi utilisation depends on timely pipeline completion
- Gopalpur terminal adds significant investment requirements
- Third jetty capex: ₹2,013 Cr
- Gopalpur terminal capex: ₹6,355 Cr

- Dahej expansion and new contracts support growth potential
- Petrochemicals offer diversification beyond regasification
- Kochi and Gopalpur provide additional utilisation opportunities
- FY27–FY29 estimates indicate modest PAT growth
- High capex and project execution remain key monitorables

US telecom stocks crashed up to 13–14% on Friday. European telecom stocks also fell 4–5%, as investors saw Elon Musk as a growing threat in that region too. 

🚨How India reacts to Reliance (Jio) and Airtel will be seen on Monday!!

- On Friday, Oct 9, Elon Musk announced that SpaceX agreed to buy a nationwide block of low-band spectrum (800 MHz) from Grain Management for reported $8 billion.

- Low-band spectrum travels farther and goes through walls/buildings/cities better.

- Combined with Starlink’s satellites (and recent approval for 15,000 more), this lets Starlink Mobile build a hybrid satellite + ground network.

- With his SpaceX will become a major full mobile carrier in the US with better coverage, including indoors. 

- Musk called it the “last critical piece” and a “very big deal.” He also described it as an “earthquake” in the spectrum world.

🚨Why US telecom stocks crashed?

- Traditional carriers (AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile) depend on expensive towers and spectrum.

- Investors feared a cash-rich SpaceX could now compete more directly and take customers or force price cuts.

- On Friday, T-Mobile down ~13%, AT&T and Verizon down ~9–10% , some of their worst days in years.

Why Europe markets also reacted:

- Same fear: Starlink’s expanding direct-to-phone capability could eventually challenge European carriers too.

- Stocks of Deutsche Telekom, Vodafone, Orange and others dropped 4–8%.

🚨Why this is a threat to Indian Telecom players like Airtel and Jio

- For Musk, India is the most lucrative large market after the US, making players like Jio and Airtel's duopoly vulnerable.

- SpaceX is sitting on a lot of cash and can move aggressively once clearances come, including his disruption and price warfare.

- Jio and Airtel dominate India’s market and have spent heavily on towers and spectrum.

- Starlink already has a licence and partnerships with them for rural areas, but full launch is still pending security and spectrum clearances.

- A working Starlink Mobile in the US proves the model works and raises the risk that Musk can disrupt pricing, coverage and the traditional tower model in India too.

Dixon signed deal with Taiwan Gemtek to make optical transceivers in India 

Dixon owns 60% of this new joint company. These are small devices that move data at high speed inside data centres and telecom networks. Gemtek knows how to make these, Dixon knows how to manufacture at scale. Same approach Dixon used before. It partnered with Nokia for broadband devices, with HKC for display screens, with Qtech for camera parts. 

Every time, Dixon picks one technology it does not have and gets it through partnership

Market for optical transceivers used in AI data centres grew 57% in 2026 to $26 billion worldwide. India buys all of these from outside right now, zero is made here. 

Dixon new Gemtek JV will start making them by early 2027. Government is also planning ₹6,000 to ₹7,000 crore support scheme for telecom component makers. Dixon has timed this move well. No other Indian electronics manufacturer has moved into this space yet. 

When data centres grow rapidly and components are fully imported, whoever starts local production first gets entire Indian demand.

Dixon makes ₹48,893 crore in annual revenue but earns only 3 to 4% margins because most of it comes from assembling products for other brands. Components like display screens, camera parts, and optical transceivers carry 6 to 7% margins. 

Dixon has been signing JVs specifically to move into component manufacturing. It partnered with HKC for displays, Qtech for cameras, and now Gemtek for optical transceivers. Management target is to raise backward integration from 15% to 40%. 

Once that happens, revenue stays similar but profit per rupee earned goes up sharply.

Just Connect the dots

The investment framework

My view of the BESS value chain:

Materials: Product differentiation and customer qualification matter.

Cells: Manufacturing scale, yields, technology and capital discipline matter.

Integration: Execution, warranty exposure and margins matter.

Grid equipment: Verify actual storage-related orders rather than assuming thematic exposure.

Asset ownership: Contract quality, financing and lifecycle economics determine returns.

Recycling: Feedstock availability and recovery economics are critical.

For smaller-company research, names such as Neogen Chemicals, Amara Raja Energy & Mobility, Pace Digitek, TCPL Packaging and SPML Infra appeared below ₹15,000 crore market capitalisation in the dated research. Their businesses and levels of BESS exposure differ, so market caps and operating developments should be rechecked before publication.

The ultimate investment framework is:
Capability → Qualification → Orders → Delivery → Cash Flow → Sustainable ROCE

India’s battery-storage opportunity is real. But a growing market is not a buy-at-any-price argument.

Follow the value captured—not just the capacity announced.

Credit : Smart Sync Investment

The biggest risks investors should monitor

A strong industry outlook does not guarantee strong shareholder returns.

Key risks include:
→ Imported raw materials and components 
→ Delayed customer qualification 
→ Underutilised manufacturing capacity 
→ Price competition and thin integration margins 
→ Warranty and performance liabilities 
→ Project delays and financing costs 
→ Working-capital pressure 
→ Technology changes 
→ Recycling feedstock shortages 
→ Expensive valuations

For every company, ask:

What is operational today? What is still planned? What generates revenue? What generates cash?

A large capacity announcement or order book cannot answer all four questions.

Recycling and next-generation battery technology

The value chain does not end when a battery is installed.

Recycling involves:
Collection → Safe transport → Dismantling → Processing → Material recovery → Reuse

Companies such as Attero and Lohum are examples of participants in India’s battery-recycling ecosystem.

However, recycling economics depend on feedstock availability, chemistry, recovery yields and the value of recovered materials.

Technology is also evolving:
→ Lithium-ion, including LFP 
→ Sodium-ion 
→ Flow batteries and other long-duration storage technologies

Different chemistries suit different applications.

The winning technology will depend on cost, safety, duration, performance and commercial viability—not simply which chemistry receives the most attention.

Government support creates demand, but not guaranteed profits

Important policy initiatives include:
→ ACC-PLI: ₹18,100 crore outlay targeting 50 GWh of advanced cell-manufacturing capacity
→ Viability Gap Funding: Two schemes supporting 43.8 GWh, with ₹9,160 crore in financial
support
→ Grid-storage procurement and tender initiatives
→ Domestic-content requirements under specified schemes

But investors must distinguish between:

Policy allocation ≠ company order
VGF support ≠ revenue
Cell-manufacturing target ≠ commissioned capacity

Project economics also depend on financing, construction, grid connection, efficiency losses,
degradation, replacement costs and contract penalties.

A large storage project can still deliver poor returns if the tariff or contract terms do not cover its full lifecycle costs.

EPC versus owning the storage asset

There are three distinct roles:

EPC contractor: Designs, procures, builds and commissions the project.

Asset owner: Invests capital and earns revenue from operating the installation.

Buyer/procurer: Contracts for storage services or electricity.

EPC businesses depend on execution, contract margins and working capital.

Asset owners depend on financing costs, utilisation, operating efficiency, degradation and long-term contract economics.

For example, ACME Solar announced an additional 437.49 MWh of commissioned BESS capacity across two Rajasthan projects on October 1, 2026, taking its reported operational BESS capacity to 4.96 GWh.

The distinction matters: announced capacity, commissioned capacity and commercial operation are not necessarily the same milestone.

The hidden opportunity: controls, cooling and power equipment

A battery container alone cannot deliver a reliable grid-storage installation.

It also needs:
→ BMS: Monitors battery conditions and helps protect operation
→ EMS: Coordinates charging, discharging and energy management
→ PCS: Converts power between the battery’s DC system and the grid’s AC system
→ Cooling and thermal management
→ Safety systems and monitoring
→ Transformers, switchgear, cables and substations

Companies such as Pace Digitek and SPML Infra offer relevant system-integration or infrastructure capabilities.

Shilchar Technologies provides transformer exposure, but its broader transformer business  should not automatically be treated as a confirmed BESS order book.

Investors should verify actual project exposure, performance guarantees, warranty obligations and replacement costs.

Cells, packs and containers are different businesses

A battery cell stores energy. A pack connects cells into a usable assembly. A container integrates batteries with controls and supporting equipment.

Do not compare their capacities as if they were interchangeable.

Key company developments from the research:
→ Exide Energy Solutions: Commissioned its 6 GWh phase-one cell facility in September
2026
→ Amara Raja: Developing its cell business and a 10 GWh BESS factory; its first giga-cell
plant was expected to commercialise in H1 FY28
→ Waaree ESS: Announced commencement of a 5.15 GWh BESS-container facility in July
2026
→ Pace Digitek: Reported 5 GWh installed manufacturing capacity, 300+ containers
delivered and 975 MWh executed through Q1 FY27

These figures represent different stages of development and execution.

The key question is whether installed capacity translates into qualified products, sales and
profits.

Battery materials: an important opportunity, but execution matters

A battery requires specialised, battery-grade materials—not simply raw minerals.

The process involves refining, manufacturing, product validation and customer qualification.

LFP batteries are particularly relevant for stationary storage because of their cost, cycle-life and safety characteristics. However, they still require lithium, graphite and other specialised inputs.

Companies to research:
→ Himadri Speciality Chemical: Anode-material development and manufacturing 
→ TACC: Demonstration-scale anode materials and planned capacity expansion 
→ Gujarat Fluorochemicals: Electrolyte salts, formulations, LFP materials and binders
→ Neogen Chemicals: Electrolytes and electrolyte salts
→ Hindalco: Battery-grade aluminium foil and related components

The opportunity is attractive, but planned capacity is not the same as commercial production.

Track: Customer qualification, production yields, repeat orders, utilisation and cash flow.

Understand the complete value chain

India’s BESS ecosystem has three broad layers.

UPSTREAM 
Minerals → Refining → Battery materials → Cells

MIDSTREAM 
Modules → Packs → Containers → Battery controls → Cooling → Power conversion

DOWNSTREAM 
Grid connection → EPC → Project ownership → Operations → Recycling

Money flows from electricity buyers and project owners to system suppliers, manufacturers and materials providers.

But each business has different margins, capital requirements and cash-flow cycles.

For example, a cell manufacturer, a container integrator and a BESS project owner are three very different investments.

Why does India need battery storage?

Solar power is strongest during daylight hours, but electricity demand continues after sunset.

Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) can store electricity and release it when required, helping manage peak demand and integrate renewable energy.

India’s 2023 National Electricity Plan projected a requirement of:
→ 47.24 GW of BESS power capacity 
→ 236 GWh of storage capacity 
→ Estimated investment of approximately ₹3.49 lakh crore by FY2031–32

Remember:
GW = power delivery capacity 
GWh = total energy storage capacity

These are planning estimates—not commissioned capacity or guaranteed orders for companies.

India’s Battery Storage Opportunity: Decoding the Entire Value Chain

India’s energy-storage opportunity is much bigger than battery manufacturing.

It spans battery materials, cells, packs, power electronics, grid equipment, project development and recycling.

With renewable energy expanding, battery storage could become a major industrial investment theme.

But the real question is: Which businesses will capture the value—and which will struggle
to earn attractive returns?

RBI comes in big with measures to defend the Rupee !

PS: I have been saying every day since the RBI policy last week, that the Rupee problem needs to be addressed.

Here is what RBI has announced,

1. The RBI is taking the PSU oil companies’ dollar demand directly onto its own book. From Oct-12, the RBI will supply the full daily dollar requirement of IOC, HPCL & BPCL via designated banks. Basically - these large, regular dollar buyers do not have to come into the market everyday & push up demand for dollars.

2. Large USD-buying hedges will now cost banks more. For certain INR derivative trades above $2 million, banks must keep 20% of the Rupee value in cash with the RBI as a reserve. That makes these trades more expensive.

3. The amount you can trade without proving you actually have an underlying FX need has been slashed. The limit has gone from $100 million to just $5 million. This applies both to OTC derivatives & exchange-traded currency derivatives.

4. You can’t cancel a Rupee FX trade & then simply put the same trade back on again ! Rollovers at maturity are still allowed. Basically meant to curb repeated trading around the same exposure.

5. You now have to certify that you haven’t hedged the same exposure somewhere else. Bascially the RBI is trying to stop the same $ requirement being used to justify multiple hedges.

- Strategic partnerships and M&A added costs.

**Long-Term Outlook**

- INR PAT CAGR projected at 6.6%.
- Forecast period covers FY27-FY29E.
- AI transformation offers potential growth opportunities.

What regulators see that investors often ignore 👇

Every time a regulator acts, investors first ask: "How much EPS gets hit?" Regulators ask something else: "Is the market structure fair for the end consumer?" That's a very different lens. 
Thoughts on recent #PBFintech & older #IEX n more

Case in point: Recent change on insurance commissions. The proposed changes effectively aim to reduce distribution costs & curb excessive upfront payouts on some products. Investors see lower margins. Regulators see lower customer acquisition costs & better value for policyholders.

Truth is, hardly anyone argues that insurance has zero mis-selling. Higher upfront commissions have often created incentives to sell what pays the most, not what suits the customer best. If that problem exists, intervention shouldn't be surprising.

The irony is that many investors celebrate efficiency in every industry except their own portfolio holdings. When a regulator targets excess distribution costs, the reaction is often outrage instead of introspection.

Look at insurance expense ratios. Even as the industry scaled up, commission/expense pools as a % of premium remained elevated in several segments. The regulator's job is to ask: why isn't scale translating into lower customer costs?

Learning from MFs TER. Every TER cut was seen as fatal attack. Prediction was: growth will die, distributors will vanish, profit collapse. Instead industry adapted. Players became efficient, direct plans gained share, technology reduced costs, investor participation & AUM surged

Market coupling in power exch. Investors focus: which exchange lose market share. Regulators focus: consumers get better price discovery. Market coupling means bids/orders from all exch get pooled to discover a single price. One price improves efficiency & reduces fragmentation

Could one exchange lose moat? Maybe. But from system perspective, better price discovery, deeper liquidity & lower market distortion are hard to ignore.
Regulators rarely optimize for shareholder returns. They optimize for consumers, market efficiency & long-term public interest

Think about hospitals. If tomorrow there is stricter price regulation, hospital stocks may get hit. As investors we'd feel the pain. But can anyone honestly deny healthcare costs are becoming unaffordable for a large section of Indians?
One may argue India's healthcare is still cheaper than many countries. True. But the person comparing prices globally is not the same person struggling to pay a hospital bill locally.

Markets often assume regulators must protect industry profitability. Regulators believe industries shouldn't fleece poor customers. When public benefit & industry profits collide, the regulator's choice is usually obvious.

That's why stock market reaction is often the last variable in the regulator's decision. If a policy improves consumer outcomes, transparency, affordability or efficiency, temporary shareholder pain rarely changes the outcome.

Tata Group Boardroom Tug of War
Some history repeat; Some history rhyme
30 yrs ago it was Ratan Tata vs Russi Mody. Today, many see shades of that battle in the Chandra vs Noel Tata face-off
Back in the 1990s, Ratan Tata was consolidating authority within a sprawling Tata empire run by powerful Operating entity heads. Russi Mody was among the most influential Tata executives of his era. Larger-than-life personality, huge public profile & massive influence within the group.
Ratan Tata believed Tata Group needed one strategic centre of gravity. Not multiple power centres running individual fiefdoms. Eventually, Russi Mody exited & Ratan Tata tightened control over the conglomerate.
Fast forward three decades.
The debate is again centred around leadership, control & the future direction of Tata Sons. This time its Noel Tata, who chairs Tata Trusts, & N Chandrasekaran, who leads Tata Sons
Key contentions are Chandra’s reappointment as chairman & Tata Sons listing. Noel Tata has opposed both
The striking part? Tata Sons board backed Chandra by a 4:1 vote, while Noel Tata stood opposed
Russi Mody took the battle public. Media interviews, public sparring & headline-grabbing exchanges became part of the story.
Chandra, however, has largely stayed silent in public
Whether history repeats or merely echoes, one thing is clear
Generational change of Tata leadership eventually confronts the same question.

Is India investing enough for future capacity

India is usually described as a consumption economy. Consumption contributes >60% of GDP. But the story becomes incomplete when we ignore what's happening on the investment side and other aspects of our economy

India's Gross Capital Formation is ~32.6% of GDP. Lower than China's ~40%, but China's per capita GDP is several times of India's. Comparing ratios without considering income levels misses the context.

A developing country cannot allocate every ₹ toward factories & infra. A large share of resources must also support the bottom of the pyramid through housing, healthcare, education & welfare.

A harmonious society requires a minimum standard of living for those at the bottom. India is building capacity while simultaneously funding social stability. That's a tougher balancing act than many realize.

So let's move beyond GDP narratives & look at hard physical data. India's share of global GDP is only ~3.5% yet produces roughly 10% of the world's steel. Steel almost 3x our weight in global GDP. Steel isn't consumed for consumption's sake, but goes into factories, rail tracks, power plants, ports, airports, infrastructure etc

Cement tells the same story. India produces ~400 MT annually out of ~4,000 MT globally. Again, roughly 10% global share despite only ~3.5% share of world GDP. Countries don't consume steel & cement at this scale unless they are building physical assets. These are the raw materials of future GDP.

Power generation presents a slightly different picture. India's share of global electricity output is lower than steel & cement, but still materially ahead of its global GDP share. India with 1800bn units vs 32,000bn units, 6% global share

The evidence suggests India is investing for future capability. One may argue the investment cycle started later than it should have, but the direction is unmistakable. Steel, Cement & Power share point toward economy preparing for a much larger future.

The scale of projects are also changing. DFCs, industrial corridors, semiconductor fabs, renewable energy parks, metros, airports, transmission corridors & logistics networks are larger than anything India attempted before.

If this trend continues, India's share of global steel, cement & power usage is likely to keep rising. Higher material intensity today is often a precursor to higher economic output tomorrow.

Maybe the better way to describe India isn't "consumption economy." It's a country simultaneously consuming, uplifting millions & building future productive capacity. 
India need a balancing act of Building future and taking care of the needy, which it is working towards

De-Dollarization lets peek into central bank reserves

Central banks are diversifying but US$ isn't giving up the throne anytime soon. Headlines scream de-dollarization bt US$ still makes up ~57% of global FX reserves. That's down from decades ago, but still miles ahead of everyone else.

Euro is the 2nd largest reserve currency at ~20%. But Europe faces weak growth, aging demographics, fiscal stress & fragmented politics. Hence no comfort for people looking to diversify away from US$

Then its China. Despite its economic size, RMB is only ~2% of global reserves & ~2% of global payments. Clear reflection of trust issues with the dragon. deep capital markets, convertibility & rule of law issues also there

They're moving into something with no issuer at all: Gold. Central banks themselves are now one of the biggest sources of gold demand globally, roughly buy ~30% of annual global mine production

Gold isn't rising only because investors are bullish. Significant chunk of global prodn is locked away by sovereign balance sheets. In 2026, central banks gold buying at slower pace vs 2025 due to 60% price rise.

Among the Major buyers were Poland, China, Brazil, India etc. 
Then there are few sellers too. Turkey has been among the largest sellers this year, reportedly selling ~83t YTD to support liquidity & FX/US$ needs.

That’s the problem. Though world want to move away from US$ in the long term but  issue in the medium term created due to lack of US$ in the country. 
Case in point Turkiye

Russia has also been a notable seller, reducing reserves by ~44t YTD as it seeks hard-currency liquidity. But Russia is also large producer of Gold

Gold is becoming a reserve diversification asset in a world where trust in fiat issuers is fragmenting.
BUT de-dollarization in reserves doesn't mean de-dollarization in trade.
That’s two very different thing

Global trade still run on the USD infrastructure. That network effect is incredibly hard to replace.
So its two-step process. Trade continues in USD.
But exporting nations convert a portion of their accumulated surplus reserves into gold, commodities, sovereign funds or other reserve assets.

The world may keep transacting in dollars while increasingly choosing not to store all its savings in dollars.

Conclusion:
Real story is different from "the end of the USD."
Reserve diversification is real.
Dollar replacement is not. Not in near future
